name: SuperCollider
comment: Strings and comments, and nothing else. This grammar is not here to colour anything — the server's semantic tokens do that, cover these same ranges, and win wherever both apply. It is here because VS Code's bracket matching, bracket-pair colouring and auto-closing read the TextMate token stream to know that a bracket inside a string or a comment is text rather than structure, and semantic tokens do not feed that path. Without it, `"("`, `$(`, `'('` and `// (` all pair with a later `)`. Every rule below delimits a literal; none of them guesses what an identifier means, which is where the grammar this replaced went wrong.

patterns.comment: A char literal, `$a` or `$\n`. Scoped under `string` rather than `constant.character` on purpose: VS Code decides a token's standard type by matching /\b(comment|string|regex|regexp)\b/ against the scope name, so only a `string` or `comment` scope suppresses the brackets inside it — and `$(` is one of the four cases this file exists for. Listed before the string and symbol rules so `$"` and `$'` are read as char literals rather than as opening a literal that never closes.
patterns.name: string.other.character.supercollider

patterns.comment: `'foo'` is a symbol, the same value `\foo` is. A bare `\foo` needs no rule: it cannot contain a bracket, so nothing depends on knowing where it ends.
patterns.name: string.quoted.single.supercollider

block-comment.comment: Block comments nest in SuperCollider — `/* /* */ */` is one comment, not a comment and a stray `*/` — so this rule includes itself.
block-comment.name: comment.block.supercollider
